analysis.title: Fed Chatterbox: October Edition
key_insights: Since the September FOMC meeting, almost all participants said further tightening will likely be needed to return inflation to 2%. Many said additional hikes are not urgent.

Waller said additional hikes "do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time." GS reads the comments as consensus for an every-other-meeting pace, which implies skipping October and hiking in December.
Chairman Warsh and President Daly indicated last week that the every-other-meeting plan remained in place after the firmer September CPI report.

Williams reiterated that "it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike" in total. Logan estimates the target range needs to rise an additional 50 basis points or more. Several participants' comments suggest they see more than one additional hike as appropriate.

Most participants are focused on underlying inflation trends and the risk that price pressures broaden. Hammack calls pressures relatively broad-based and not just from the supply side, citing AI-buildout demand for computer, electronic and high-tech components.

Goolsbee said the Fed may need to consider responding to persistent supply shocks. Williams said measures of underlying inflation have come down, and Jefferson said no spillovers from tariffs, energy shocks and goods prices into broader inflation were yet visible. Both comments predate last week's CPI report.
Almost all participants share Williams's view that the labor market is basically in balance and not adding inflationary pressures.

Bowman (Oct 14) sees time to wait and see how financial conditions and the economy evolve and feels no urgency for further action. Kashkari (Sep 30) sees value in slow adjustments and is questioning how tight policy is.
Musalem (Oct 8) said rates ought to go up further over the next 6-9 months. Collins (Oct 13) expects it will be appropriate to raise rates a bit further before year-end.
Waller said he is not greatly concerned that tighter policy threatens a damaging slowdown, given evidence that activity is strengthening in the second half.
Barr counts only two months of data consistent with 2% core PCE inflation over the past 20 months and sees no clear trend toward a timely return to 2%.

Paulson put underlying inflation at about 2.5 to 3 percent and said the AI buildout is one factor keeping it high. Barkin said inflation more than a percentage point above target is a problem, but is open to the possibility that some shocks reverse.

macro_indicators.reading: One more hike (Williams); additional 50 bp or more (Logan)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Officials differ on the terminal rate. GS reads several comments as favoring more than one additional hike.

macro_indicators.reading: Skip October, hike in December (every-other-meeting pace)
macro_indicators.interpretation: GS reads Waller, Warsh and Daly comments as a consensus for hiking every other meeting.
Well above the 2% target, with the gap showing little sign of closing, according to Paulson.

macro_indicators.reading: More than a percentage point above target (Barkin)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Barkin calls this a problem, since passing shocks are not proving short-lived.

macro_indicators.reading: Only two months consistent with 2% over the past 20 months (Barr)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Barr sees no clear trend toward a timely return to 2%.

risk_factors: Broadening of inflation pressures or second-round effects from negative supply shocks and persistent demand pressures (Musalem).
AI buildout demand raising prices on computer, electronic and high-tech components, with costs spreading to aviation, electricity production and construction (Hammack).
Demand overheating from AI data center construction and elevated services inflation (Goolsbee).
Higher oil prices and supply chain disruptions tied to the Middle East conflict (Cook).
New tariffs from continuing trade conflicts (Waller).
An inflationary mindset taking hold could require more tightening than otherwise (Hammack).
geopolitical: Waller cited fading hopes for a quick end to the Middle East conflict as undermining his faith in inflation progress.
Williams and Cook cite supply-chain disruptions and higher energy and commodity prices from conflicts in the Middle East.
Waller cited continuing trade conflicts that threaten new tariffs.

tension_points.bull_case: Hawkish officials (Logan, Musalem, Hammack, Collins) say more tightening is needed. Logan puts it at 50 basis points or more, and Hammack sees broad-based inflation that will take time to fall.
tension_points.bear_case: Williams says one more hike may suffice and that underlying inflation measures have come down. Bowman and Kashkari favor patience and slow adjustments, and Jefferson sees no spillovers into broader inflation.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence that price pressures broaden beyond energy and AI-buildout categories would favor the hawks. Williams's and Jefferson's comments predate last week's firmer CPI report.
